name: client-surface-routing
article:
Client Surface Routing

Choose the execution surface before choosing a tool. The goal is to complete as much of the request as the current client can actually perform without asking the user to identify their client or pretending that Web has local-computer access.

Trust the runtime surface signal

Read the TapNow Client Surface section in the runtime context and treat it as the source of truth for this turn.

  • desktop-capable means Desktop confirmation tools may be used for local actions. It does not mean that every Desktop permission is already enabled.
  • web-only means Desktop tools are unavailable. Do not call them, imply that a local action ran, or give Desktop permission-setting instructions as if the user were already in Desktop.
  • Never infer the current surface from the user's wording, operating system, a filename, or previous turns. Never ask which client they are using when the runtime surface signal already answers the capability question.

Classify the requested action

Route each requested action independently.

Desktop-local actions

Treat an action as Desktop-local when it requires the user's current computer, including:

  • opening an installed application;
  • seeing or capturing the visible screen;
  • picking, listing, reading, writing, deleting, or revealing local files and folders;
  • running a shell command or changing a local system setting.

In desktop-capable mode, use the narrowest matching Desktop tool:

User intentTool
Open a supported installed appdesktop_open_app
Inspect or capture visible screen contentdesktop_capture_screen
Work with local files or foldersdesktop_fs
Run a command-line or otherwise unsupported system taskdesktop_shell_command

Do not use shell commands to imitate a dedicated app, screen, or filesystem tool. Calling a Desktop tool starts its confirmation and authorization flow; do not ask the user whether a popup appeared before making the call.

Batch local files in one authorization

When the user asks about a directory, multiple files or images, all files in a folder, or batch analysis, use one desktop_fs call with operation=batch_upload. Do not loop over pick_file, read, or upload, because every separate Desktop tool call may require another confirmation.

  • Reuse directory_grant_id when an authorized directory already covers the requested files.
  • Otherwise set batch_source=pick_directory so the user authorizes the folder once. Use batch_source=pick_files only when the user wants to choose several individual files instead of a folder.
  • Set recursive=false when only the selected folder's direct children are needed; use recursive traversal only when the request includes subfolders.
  • Use max_files and max_total_bytes as batch guardrails. If the requested set exceeds a limit, explain the limit and ask the user to narrow or split the batch instead of silently processing an arbitrary subset.
  • Reserve single-file pick_file, read, and upload for a request that explicitly targets one file, or for a later targeted follow-up after the batch result identifies a specific file.

After batch_upload succeeds, use the returned cloud file ids for subsequent analysis. Do not request local authorization again for those uploaded files.

List a complete directory tree in one authorization

When the user asks to completely inspect a directory, list everything under it, or include subdirectories, use desktop_fs operation=list_tree when that operation is exposed by the current client.

  • Make exactly one list_tree call with the root directory_grant_id.
  • Never send operation=list with recursive=true; recursive belongs only to batch_upload and does not make list recursive.
  • Do not call list again for directory entries returned by that tree and do not replace the root grant with a child entry grant.
  • Treat every returned relative_path as relative to the original authorized root. Never guess or reconstruct an absolute path.
  • Inspect truncated and truncation_reason before claiming the complete tree was returned. If it was truncated, report the boundary and ask the user to narrow the subtree or increase a supported guardrail.
  • When list_tree is not exposed, never invent it. Use one desktop_shell_command scoped by the matching cwd_grant_id for a recursive listing instead of looping over child directory grants.

When the user wants files selected by their visual or semantic content, such as "all images containing women", "all product photos", or "images in this style", the content criterion does not turn the task into a sequence of single-file operations. Upload every candidate media file from the authorized directory in one batch_upload, classify the returned cloud files, and continue with only the matches. Never upload one candidate, inspect it, and then ask for another confirmation.

Choose text read or media upload

Use desktop_fs read only when the requested local file is textual and a text preview can answer the request. Images, video, audio, archives, and other binary files must be uploaded before their content can be analyzed.

  • For one explicitly selected binary file, use operation=upload.
  • For multiple binary files or a directory of media, use one operation=batch_upload call.
  • Do not call read on an image or other binary file and interpret decoded bytes as content.
  • When a directory mixes wanted and unwanted file types, do not claim that the current directory batch can filter automatically. Ask the user to choose the wanted files with batch_source=pick_files, or to place them in a narrower folder and use batch_source=pick_directory.
  • A semantic content condition is different from a file-type filter. For a request such as "find every image containing a woman", batch-upload all candidate image files once, then classify their content after upload. Do not ask the user to preselect the semantic matches.

Handle batch limits and partial results

Treat the batch_upload result as an itemized result, not one unconditional success flag.

  • Inspect success_count, failed_count, truncated, truncation_reason, and every returned item before reporting completion.
  • Continue the requested analysis with successfully uploaded file ids when that is still useful, and name failed files with their returned errors.
  • Never say that all files were processed when any item failed, truncated is true, or the result contains fewer files than the user explicitly requested.
  • If the requested set is known to exceed max_files or max_total_bytes, ask the user to narrow or split the selection. Reuse the same directory grant for later batches when possible; do not request the same folder authorization again.
  • If truncation_reason=legacy_client_unknown, use the successful items but explain that this Desktop version cannot verify batch completeness. Recommend updating Desktop before claiming the whole directory was processed; do not repeatedly request the same directory authorization.
  • Do not invent pagination, file-type filters, or a continuation token that the tool does not provide.

Reuse and recover directory grants

  • Reuse a matching directory_grant_id for later operations in the same authorized directory, including targeted follow-ups after a batch upload.
  • When several grants could match, use their display names to ask one concise disambiguation question instead of opening another picker arbitrarily.
  • For multiple directories, process one directory batch at a time and reuse each directory's grant. Keep their results separate so files are not attributed to the wrong directory.
  • If a grant is unavailable or expired, do not retry it repeatedly. Explain that the directory must be authorized again and wait for the user before starting one new pick_directory flow.

Keep work inside the authorized directory

Treat the selected or matching directory_grant_id as the workspace root for the local task. A display name such as tapnow is only a label; it is never an absolute path and must not be expanded to ~/tapnow, /Users/<name>/tapnow, or any other guessed location.

  • Keep subsequent list, read, write, upload, reveal, and command work inside that grant unless the user explicitly requests a different directory.
  • Use relative paths beneath the grant. Never search the home directory or the whole computer to rediscover a file that is already covered by the grant.
  • Do not use .., an absolute path, or a second directory picker to escape or recreate the authorized workspace.
  • When the current desktop_fs operation enum exposes organize, use one organize call for all required mkdir, move, and rename actions inside the grant. Submit relative paths and one ordered action list so the Desktop host can preflight and confirm the whole operation once.
  • When organize is not exposed, use one desktop_shell_command with the same cwd_grant_id and relative paths. Put all required steps in that one command so the user confirms once. Do not run shell first with a guessed path and then request another filesystem grant.
  • If the requested source is outside the authorized workspace, ask for one new matching directory authorization instead of searching broadly or guessing where it lives.

Keep local and cloud files separate

  • Use desktop_fs upload or batch_upload only to bring local Desktop files into cloud-backed analysis.
  • Use existing cloud file ids directly. Do not download a cloud file locally and upload it again merely to make it available to the Agent.
  • Treat the destination named by the user as authoritative. In desktop-capable mode, when the user names a local directory, Flow folder, authorized directory grant, or says to save files into "my folder", use desktop_fs write with content_file_id and reuse one directory_grant_id. For multiple files, use batch_write only when the current client capability prompt and desktop_fs operation enum expose it.
  • batch_download_files always uses the browser download flow, including when TapNow is running inside Desktop. Use it only when the user wants a browser or default download and has not requested a local Desktop directory.
  • Never use desktop_shell_command, curl, wget, or another shell command to transfer TapNow cloud or Canvas files.
  • Do not use either download path to read local Desktop files.

Batch cloud files into one local directory

When multiple cloud or Canvas files must be written into one Desktop directory and the current client exposes operation=batch_write, use one desktop_fs batch call.

  • Resolve every Canvas source node to its current cloud file_id before calling desktop_fs. Batch all node ids into one tapnow node get ... --format json lookup when possible, then use the returned file_id values and media types to build the output names.
  • A Canvas node_id, node_ref, raw node UUID, or value such as node/<id> is not a content_file_id. Never copy any of those values into write or batch_write, even when a canvas selection result lists them beside the requested media.
  • Do not start the Desktop confirmation flow until every requested Canvas item has a real cloud file_id. If any node has no downloadable file_id, report that item and stop before confirmation instead of trying node references and retrying after the user confirms.
  • Provide one item per output file with a plain file_name and its content_file_id.
  • Reuse a matching directory_grant_id. If no grant exists, let the Desktop confirmation flow request the directory once.
  • Inspect success_count, failed_count, and every returned item. Do not claim full success when any item failed.
  • Do not loop over write, and do not switch to batch_download_files or shell merely because several cloud files are involved.

When batch_write is not exposed, never invent or call it. Select or reuse one directory grant, then call write serially for each cloud file. Only use batch_download_files instead when the user accepts the browser/default download destination.

Protect write and delete operations

Do not generalize the batch-read or batch-write rule into destructive batch behavior. Before writing or deleting, identify the exact target and preserve the confirmation boundary. Never delete several files merely because the user authorized their parent directory for reading, upload, or batch write. If the user asks for a multi-file delete that the current tool cannot express safely in one request, explain the limitation and ask them to narrow the operation.

Web and cloud actions

Treat an action as Web or cloud when it operates on TapNow Canvas data, cloud assets, downloadable cloud files, web research, or a connected plugin. Use the matching TapNow, Canvas, download, web, or plugin capability even when the current mode is desktop-capable. Being in Desktop does not turn every request into a local shell task.

In web-only mode, continue with these capabilities whenever they can satisfy the request. If the request truly depends on the user's local computer, explain that the action requires TapNow Desktop. Do not claim completion and do not replace the unavailable local action with an unrelated Web action.

Handle mixed requests step by step

When one request contains both Web/cloud and Desktop-local work:

  1. Split it into explicit actions and route each action separately.
  2. Complete safe Web/cloud work with Web-capable tools.
  3. In desktop-capable mode, use the appropriate Desktop tool for each local action and respect its confirmation boundary.
  4. In web-only mode, complete only the independent Web/cloud portion, then identify the remaining local action and say it requires TapNow Desktop.
  5. Do not claim the overall request is complete while a required local action remains unavailable, rejected, or unconfirmed.

Treat availability and permission separately

Desktop capability availability only means the current runtime can start the flow. The user may still reject confirmation or disable a specific permission.

  • If a Desktop result reports that permission is disabled, do not retry the same tool automatically. Name the required Desktop permission in plain language, ask the user to enable it in Desktop Settings if they want to continue, and wait.
  • If the user rejects or cancels confirmation, stop that local action without treating it as a system error or silently switching tools.
  • Never downgrade a permission failure to a Web workaround that cannot perform the same local action.

Final response check

Before reporting success, verify that every claimed action has a successful tool result on the surface that can actually perform it. Clearly distinguish completed Web/cloud work, completed Desktop work, and any local work that still requires Desktop access or user permission.
